column2: The standardized test statistic for a one-sample z-test for a proportion measures:
column3: How many standard deviations the sample proportion is from the null hypothesis value
column4: How many standard deviations the sample proportion is from the sample mean value
column5: The probability that the null hypothesis is true given the observed sample data
column6: The probability of getting the observed sample proportion in any random sample

column2: The formula for the standardized test statistic in a one-sample z-test for a proportion is:
column3: z = (p-hat minus p0) divided by the square root of p0 times (1 minus p0) divided by n
column4: z = (p-hat minus p0) divided by the square root of p-hat times (1 minus p-hat) divided by n
column5: z = (p0 minus p-hat) divided by the square root of p-hat times (1 minus p-hat) divided by n
column6: z = (p-hat minus p0) divided by the square root of p0 times (1 minus p0) divided by n squared

column2: In the denominator of the test statistic formula, we use p0 instead of p-hat because:
column3: We assume the null hypothesis is true when performing the calculations for a significance test
column4: We assume the alternative hypothesis is true when performing the calculations for a test
column5: The formula sheet requires p0 in the denominator but either value would produce the same answer
column6: Using p-hat would make the test statistic too large and give misleading results every time

column2: The general form of a standardized test statistic is:
column3: (statistic minus null value of parameter) divided by the standard deviation of the statistic
column4: (null value of parameter minus statistic) divided by the standard deviation of the statistic
column5: (statistic minus null value of parameter) divided by the sample size used in the study
column6: (statistic minus sample mean) divided by the standard error of the sample mean

column2: In the lemonade study (n=30, p-hat=0.60, p0=0.50), the test statistic z equals:
column3: 1.10, because (0.60 minus 0.50) divided by the square root of (0.50 times 0.50 divided by 30) equals 1.10
column4: 2.00, because (0.60 minus 0.50) divided by the square root of (0.60 times 0.40 divided by 30) equals 2.00
column5: 0.10, because the numerator of the test statistic is simply 0.60 minus 0.50 which equals 0.10
column6: 1.50, because (0.60 minus 0.50) divided by the square root of (0.50 times 0.50 divided by 50) equals 1.50

column2: A z-score of 1.10 in the lemonade study means the sample proportion of 0.60 is:
column3: About 1.1 standard deviations above the null hypothesis value of 0.50 — not that unusual
column4: About 1.1 standard deviations below the null hypothesis value of 0.50 — very unusual
column5: Exactly 1.1 percentage points away from the null hypothesis value of 0.50
column6: More than two standard deviations above the null hypothesis value which is very unusual

column2: In the football study (n=100, p-hat=0.29, p0=0.40), the test statistic z equals:
column3: Negative 2.25, because (0.29 minus 0.40) divided by the square root of (0.40 times 0.60 divided by 100)
column4: Positive 2.25, because (0.40 minus 0.29) divided by the square root of (0.40 times 0.60 divided by 100)
column5: Negative 1.10, because (0.29 minus 0.40) divided by the square root of (0.29 times 0.71 divided by 100)
column6: Negative 2.50, because (0.29 minus 0.40) divided by the square root of (0.50 times 0.50 divided by 100)

column2: A z-score of negative 2.25 in the football study means the sample proportion of 0.29 is:
column3: More than two standard deviations below the null hypothesis value of 0.40 — pretty unusual
column4: More than two standard deviations above the null hypothesis value of 0.40 — pretty unusual
column5: Less than one standard deviation below the null hypothesis value of 0.40 — not that unusual
column6: Exactly 2.25 percentage points below the null hypothesis value of 0.40

column2: The p-value of a significance test is defined as:
column3: The probability of getting evidence for Ha as strong as or stronger than the observed evidence by chance alone when H0 is true
column4: The probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data that were observed in the sample
column5: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true given the data that were observed
column6: The probability of making an error when rejecting the null hypothesis based on sample data

column2: The p-value is calculated assuming that:
column3: The null hypothesis is true — it measures how surprising the data would be under that assumption
column4: The alternative hypothesis is true — it measures how likely we are to confirm the research question
column5: Neither hypothesis is true — it measures the probability of each hypothesis being correct
column6: Both hypotheses are equally likely — it measures which one the data support more strongly

column2: When the alternative hypothesis is Ha: p > p0, the p-value is found by calculating:
column3: The area to the right of the observed test statistic under the standard normal curve
column4: The area to the left of the observed test statistic under the standard normal curve
column5: The area in both tails of the standard normal curve beyond the observed test statistic
column6: The area between the observed test statistic and zero under the standard normal curve

column2: When the alternative hypothesis is Ha: p < p0, the p-value is found by calculating:
column3: The area to the left of the observed test statistic under the standard normal curve
column4: The area to the right of the observed test statistic under the standard normal curve
column5: The area in both tails of the standard normal curve beyond the observed test statistic
column6: The total area under the standard normal curve minus the area at the test statistic

column2: When the alternative hypothesis is Ha: p is not equal to p0, the p-value is found by calculating:
column3: Two times the area in one tail of the standard normal curve beyond the observed test statistic
column4: The area in one tail of the standard normal curve beyond the observed test statistic
column5: The area between negative z and positive z under the standard normal curve
column6: The area to the right of the observed test statistic only, since we always use the right tail

column2: For the lemonade study with Ha: p > 0.50 and z = 1.10, the p-value equals:
column3: 0.1357, which is the area to the right of z = 1.10 under the standard normal curve
column4: 0.8643, which is the area to the left of z = 1.10 under the standard normal curve
column5: 0.2714, which is two times the area to the right of z = 1.10 under the standard normal curve
column6: 0.1357, which is the area to the left of z = 1.10 under the standard normal curve

column2: For the football study with Ha: p not equal to 0.40 and z = negative 2.25, the p-value equals:
column3: 0.0244, which is two times the area in one tail because this is a two-sided test
column4: 0.0122, which is just the area to the left of z = negative 2.25 in one tail
column5: 0.9878, which is the area to the right of z = negative 2.25 under the standard normal curve
column6: 0.0488, which is four times the area in one tail for a two-sided test

column2: Why does a two-sided test use both tails when calculating the p-value?
column3: Because evidence on either side of the null value supports the alternative when Ha uses not-equal-to
column4: Because the null hypothesis could be true on either side of the alternative hypothesis value
column5: Because the standard normal curve is symmetric and we must always account for both halves
column6: Because using only one tail would make the p-value too small and lead to incorrect decisions

column2: The formula sheet on the AP exam provides the standardized test statistic as:
column3: (statistic minus parameter) divided by the standard error of the statistic
column4: (parameter minus statistic) divided by the standard deviation of the parameter
column5: (statistic minus parameter) divided by the sample size used in the study
column6: (statistic plus parameter) divided by the standard error of the statistic

column2: On the AP formula sheet, for the random variable p-hat (single proportion), the standard deviation formula uses p while the standard error formula uses p-hat. For a significance test, we use:
column3: The standard deviation formula with p0 substituted for p because we assume H0 is true
column4: The standard error formula with p-hat because it comes from the actual sample data collected
column5: Either formula because both produce the same result for any significance test about a proportion
column6: The standard error formula because the AP exam always requires the standard error version

column2: When interpreting a p-value, you MUST include a statement that:
column3: The null hypothesis is assumed to be true as the starting condition for the probability
column4: The alternative hypothesis is assumed to be true as the starting condition for the probability
column5: The sample was randomly selected from the population of interest for the study
column6: The conditions for inference have been verified before performing the significance test

column2: When interpreting a p-value, you must state the probability of getting a result:
column3: As extreme as or more extreme than the observed value, not just exactly equal to it
column4: Exactly equal to the observed value, since that is the specific outcome in the sample
column5: Less extreme than the observed value, since we want to know how common the result is
column6: Within one standard deviation of the observed value to capture the likely range of outcomes

column2: When interpreting a p-value, you should include the phrase:
column3: By chance alone — indicating the result could occur due to random sampling variability
column4: By statistical significance — indicating the result is meaningful and important
column5: By hypothesis testing — indicating the result was obtained through a formal test procedure
column6: By normal approximation — indicating the result relies on the normal distribution

column2: A correct interpretation of the lemonade study p-value of 0.1357 is:
column3: Assuming 50% of all students would choose the green cup, there is a 0.1357 probability of getting a sample proportion of 0.60 or greater by chance alone in a random sample of 30 students
column4: There is a 13.57% probability that the true proportion of students who would choose the green cup is exactly 0.50
column5: There is an 86.43% probability that more than 50% of all students would choose the green cup over the white cup
column6: The sample proportion of 0.60 proves that 13.57% of the time the null hypothesis will be rejected

column2: A student says the p-value of 0.1357 means there is a 13.57% chance that H0 is true. This is:
column3: Incorrect — the p-value assumes H0 is true and measures how surprising the data would be under H0
column4: Correct — the p-value directly tells us the probability that the null hypothesis is true
column5: Incorrect — the p-value is actually the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true instead
column6: Correct — but only when the test is one-sided, not when it is a two-sided significance test

column2: You can think of a p-value as a:
column3: Conditional probability, where the condition is that the null hypothesis is true
column4: Conditional probability, where the condition is that the alternative hypothesis is true
column5: Joint probability of both the null hypothesis being true and the data being observed together
column6: Marginal probability that does not depend on any assumptions about the hypotheses at all

column2: For the football study (two-sided), the p-value interpretation must include the phrase:
column3: In either direction — because evidence above or below the null value supports Ha when Ha uses not-equal-to
column4: In one direction — because the sample proportion was only below the null hypothesis value of 0.40
column5: In the positive direction — because we always interpret p-values in the direction of larger values
column6: In the negative direction — because the z-score was negative 2.25 and we follow the sign of z

column2: A smaller p-value provides:
column3: Stronger evidence against the null hypothesis because the observed result would be more surprising if H0 were true
column4: Weaker evidence against the null hypothesis because smaller numbers always indicate less importance
column5: Stronger evidence for the null hypothesis because a small probability means H0 is likely to be true
column6: No information about the strength of evidence because p-values do not measure evidence strength

column2: Comparing the lemonade p-value (0.1357) to the football p-value (0.0244), we can say:
column3: The football study provides stronger evidence against H0 because a smaller p-value means the result is less likely under H0
column4: The lemonade study provides stronger evidence against H0 because a larger p-value means more data supports Ha
column5: Both studies provide the same strength of evidence because both are testing claims about proportions
column6: The studies cannot be compared because one is one-sided and the other is two-sided

column2: If a test statistic is farther from zero (larger in absolute value), the p-value will be:
column3: Smaller, because the observed result is farther from the null value and more unusual under H0
column4: Larger, because the observed result is farther from the null value and more common under H0
column5: The same, because the p-value does not depend on the magnitude of the test statistic at all
column6: Either larger or smaller depending on whether the test is one-sided or two-sided

column2: The numerator of the test statistic (p-hat minus p0) measures:
column3: The difference between the observed sample proportion and the hypothesized population proportion
column4: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion
column5: The probability that the observed sample proportion is different from the null hypothesis value
column6: The number of standard deviations between the sample statistic and the population parameter

column2: The denominator of the test statistic sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n) represents:
column3: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p-hat when the null hypothesis is true
column4: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p-hat when the alternative is true
column5: The margin of error for a confidence interval for the population proportion
column6: The standard error of p-hat calculated using the observed sample proportion

column2: If H0: p = 0.30 and n = 200, and p-hat = 0.25, the test statistic z equals:
column3: Negative 1.54, calculated as (0.25 minus 0.30) divided by the square root of (0.30 times 0.70 divided by 200)
column4: Negative 1.63, calculated as (0.25 minus 0.30) divided by the square root of (0.25 times 0.75 divided by 200)
column5: Positive 1.54, calculated as (0.30 minus 0.25) divided by the square root of (0.30 times 0.70 divided by 200)
column6: Negative 2.00, calculated as (0.25 minus 0.30) divided by the square root of (0.50 times 0.50 divided by 200)

column2: For the test in the previous question with Ha: p < 0.30 and z = negative 1.54, the p-value is approximately:
column3: 0.0618 — the area to the left of z = negative 1.54 because Ha is less than
column4: 0.9382 — the area to the right of z = negative 1.54 because we want the larger area
column5: 0.1236 — two times the area in one tail because this is a two-sided significance test

column2: If a one-sided test produces a p-value of 0.03, then a two-sided test with the same data would produce a p-value of:
column3: 0.06, because a two-sided p-value is found by doubling the one-tail area
column4: 0.03, because the p-value is the same regardless of whether the test is one-sided or two-sided
column5: 0.015, because a two-sided test splits the p-value equally between the two tails
column6: 0.09, because a two-sided test adds the p-value from three different regions of the curve

column2: After calculating the test statistic using the formula, we find the p-value by using:
column3: A standard normal distribution (z-distribution), because the test statistic follows this distribution when conditions are met
column4: A t-distribution with n minus one degrees of freedom, because the population proportion is unknown
column5: A chi-square distribution, because we are testing a claim about a single population proportion
column6: A binomial distribution, because the data involve counting successes and failures in a sample

column2: A test statistic of z = 0 would mean that:
column3: The sample proportion exactly equals the null hypothesis value, so p-hat equals p0
column4: The null hypothesis is definitely true and there is no need to calculate a p-value
column5: The alternative hypothesis is definitely false and should be rejected immediately
column6: The conditions for the test were not met and the result is invalid for inference

column2: If z = 0 for a one-sided test (Ha: p > p0), the p-value would be:
column3: 0.50, because half the area under the standard normal curve is above z = 0
column4: 1.00, because all of the area under the standard normal curve is above or below z = 0
column5: 0.00, because there is no evidence against the null hypothesis when z equals zero
column6: 0.05, because that is the standard significance level used for all hypothesis tests

column2: The information needed to calculate the test statistic for a one-sample z-test includes:
column3: The sample proportion (p-hat), the null hypothesis value (p0), and the sample size (n)
column4: The sample proportion (p-hat), the alternative hypothesis value, and the population size (N)
column5: The sample proportion (p-hat), the confidence level, and the margin of error for the interval
